questions.text: Process Definition
Process boundaries
Employee functions and roles
Customer-oriented business processes
Process Measures
Governance role
Decision-making practices
Process improvement practices
Information technology
Process Culture
Departments are provided with complete information needed to carry out their activities.
Departments are provided with the information needed to carry out their activities in a timely manner.
Employees from different departments fully trust one another.
Employees feel uncomfortable asking another department for help when necessary.
Employees from different departments easily schedule meetings with one another when necessary.
Departments often blame each other when an issue is not resolved or fails.
Conflicts between different departments are frequent.
When members of different departments come together, tension increases.
In general, people in one department dislike interacting with representatives of other departments.
Conflict between representatives of different departments rarely occurs in the company.

answers.text: The company has no formal documentation of processes at all, or it is very limited.
Processes are documented in a fragmented way and mostly reflect the internal activities of individual departments.

All important cross-functional processes in the company (involving two or more departments) are described, documented, and standardized. Documentation follows a single standard agreed upon across the entire company.

Process documentation is managed through a stable and organized practice, with formal rules and methods that ensure descriptions are updated in a timely manner, version-controlled, stored, and quickly shared with relevant stakeholders.

Electronic platforms such as a Business Process Management Suite (BPMS) are used for process modeling and documentation, integrated with the company's various systems. This enables simulation-based process analysis, rapid updating of descriptions, cross-functional collaboration, and easy accessibility.
The activities of employees and/or departments are often unclear and change spontaneously or situationally.
The boundaries of employees' or departments' activities are defined, but the points of interaction between them are not clearly defined or standardized.
Within the company, collaboration, coordination, and points of interaction between departments are clearly defined and standardized.

Service levels between departments and teams are agreed in advance, for example response time and quality. The company has also established a mechanism for consistently managing these agreements and process boundaries.

Process boundaries are flexible and adaptable to changes in the business environment and external factors. Based on real-time information, the company can quickly adjust process boundaries and resource allocation.
Functions and duties are not clearly distributed among employees — more or less, "everyone does everything."
Employee functions and roles are more or less distributed and defined according to the company's departments.
Employee roles and functions are clearly defined and understood consistently across the company.
Employee functions and roles are defined based on the analysis and design of cross-functional processes, ensuring that process goals and tasks are fulfilled.

Employee roles and job design are dynamic and adapt as closely as possible to environmental changes. Participating in process improvement teams and identifying and sharing best practices is one of employees' formal functions.
Decisions in the company are made mainly intuitively and spontaneously, mostly by the company's director.
The company has no clear, agreed-upon understanding of who "our end customers" are. Customer needs are taken into account unsystematically.

Key suppliers and customer segments are clearly identified and understood by everyone in the company. Although customer needs are taken into account, the company is mainly focused on its internal operations.
Customer needs are known and precisely defined in terms of what customers want or require. Process modeling and design are carried out according to customer needs.
The company has implemented structured mechanisms for collecting customer feedback. The information received is actively used for process analysis and improvement.

Information about customer experience and satisfaction is collected in real time in relevant electronic systems. Customer feedback is one of the main sources for the continuous improvement of processes and products.
The company has no performance indicators for its activities, and no corresponding monitoring is carried out.
Performance in the company is mostly assessed using financial indicators (cost/revenue), although these indicators are not used regularly to measure performance.
Process performance and results are measured and assessed using indicators in the company.

Process performance is measured and managed using statistical and quantitative methods. Indicators are used to manage performance and optimize processes. Indicators are regularly modeled based on the company's strategic goals.

Performance indicators are monitored in real time using advanced analytics technologies, such as Business Activity Monitoring (BAM) systems, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) algorithms. These indicators make it possible to identify and resolve problems in advance.
The roles and functions of employees and management are not clearly separated in the company. Governance is mostly informal.
Departments have managers with defined functions and duties who oversee the internal activities of the department.
Each cross-functional process (involving two or more departments) has a process owner who is responsible for the process's results.

The organization has implemented a consistent business process management practice. The process owner's role is clear and includes process analysis, optimization, planning, resource provisioning, and performance monitoring.

The process owner actively encourages team members to test new ideas and contribute to the continuous improvement of processes. The process owner is one of the main architects of the continuous improvement culture.

Important decisions in the company are made more often based on qualitative assessments than on the analysis of quantitative data. Decisions are mainly made by the director, but are sometimes delegated to managers depending on the situation.

Quantitative information obtained from the company's processes is actively used to make important operational decisions. Standard decisions required for process execution are, to some extent, automated and integrated into the IT system.
Predictive/prescriptive analytics are used to make decisions. Most of the standard decisions required for process execution are automated and carried out through the IT system.
Decisions are made based on in-depth modeling and analysis of existing information and data. Standard decisions required for business processes are clearly delegated to middle management.
The company has no established practice of process improvement, or if it exists, it is fragmented and inconsistent.
In the organization, department managers are more focused on optimizing their own operations than on improving cross-functional processes.

Process improvement is carried out through cross-functional teams. Various methodologies are used (Six Sigma, Lean, Agile, and others), although the organization has not implemented a unified and systematic practice.

The company has implemented a systematic methodology for process development (e.g., Lean, Six Sigma, the Rummler-Brache methodology, etc.). The effectiveness of improvements is measured by quantitative indicators aligned with the company's strategic goals.
Information obtained from existing IT systems about customer experience and process performance is actively used for process improvement. The improvement cycle is continuous, fast, and dynamic.
Information technologies are used to a limited extent in the company.
The IT systems in the company are fragmented and poorly integrated.
The company's IT systems support the effective execution of cross-functional processes.
The company's IT systems are integrated and serve as an important source for identifying and improving processes.

Various technologies, including Robotic Process Automation (RPA), artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML), are integrated into business processes to automate routine tasks and increase the ability to make effective decisions.
The company's management has limited understanding of what business process management is.
Management recognizes the need to improve operational activities/business processes, but knowledge of business processes is inconsistent and limited.
The company's employees have a consistent understanding of business processes and comply with established standards.
Business process management is part of management's daily activities. Managers actively use business-process-related terminology (e.g., input, output, process owner, waste).
Process improvement is also part of employees' daily activities. They actively generate process improvement ideas, and identify and share good work practices.
